body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"The contact evaluation cascade for pulmonary tuberculosis in a metropolitan health department","authors":"Oyelaran-Whitfield J, Castellanos-Mbeki R, Lindahl-Osei P","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Tuberculosis Program Practice","doi":"10.5555/jtpp.2021.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Of 3,120 contacts identified for 262 pulmonary tuberculosis cases in one metropolitan health department, 88 percent were located, 79 percent had a test, and 68 percent completed evaluation. The largest losses occurred between a positive test and the chest radiograph, and among contacts living in shelters or working night shifts. Median time from contact identification to completed evaluation was 38 days. Contacts evaluated at home completed more often than those referred to clinics. The authors recommend reporting every step of the cascade rather than a single completion figure."},{"title":"Blood draw at the first home visit for tuberculosis contacts: a program report","authors":"City tuberculosis control program, Brackenmoor health unit","year":null,"venue":"Public health program report series","providerType":"report","abstract":"The program began drawing blood for interferon-gamma release assays at the first home visit instead of referring contacts to a clinic. The report states that completion of testing rose from 74 to 91 percent after the change, and that nurses spent more time per visit. It gives no dates for the before and after periods, no denominators by contact type and no information on whether chest radiographs were completed. Staff comments describe fewer lost samples once courier pickup was arranged."},{"title":"Lean redesign of latent tuberculosis evaluation in a public health clinic","authors":"Nakamura-Holt S, Achebe-Fairweather T","year":2019,"venue":"Lean Methods in Public Health","doi":"10.5555/lmph.2019.0058","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A public health clinic mapped the value stream of contact evaluation and found 11 handoffs between identification and completed evaluation. After redesign (same-day testing, results routed to the case nurse, radiograph booked at the result visit), median days from contact identification to completed evaluation fell from 41 to 19, and completion within 60 days rose from 66 to 82 percent over 12 months. Nurse time per contact rose slightly, and staff reported fewer calls chasing results. The comparison was before and after, with no concurrent control."},{"title":"Interpreter use and completion of tuberculosis contact evaluation: an internal review","authors":"Community health nursing quality group","year":null,"venue":"Internal quality review","providerType":"report","abstract":"This internal review of one year of contact investigations found that contacts who needed an interpreter completed evaluation in 58 percent of cases, against 77 percent of other contacts. Telephone interpreters were used for most phone calls, but not at clinic visits for blood draws. The review does not give its year, and it did not adjust for household status, shelter residence or distance to the clinic. It recommends booking interpreters for every step, not only the first call, and recording each contact's preferred language at the first contact."},{"title":"Interventions to improve completion of tuberculosis contact investigation: a systematic review","authors":"Rasmussen-Oduya E, Petit-Kowalczyk M, Sato-Brennan L, Varga-Okafor D","year":2023,"venue":"Tuberculosis Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/ter.2023.0091","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 22 studies of interventions to improve completion of contact investigation, including home-based testing, incentives, text reminders and case management. Home-based testing and incentives raised completion by a median of 12 percentage points compared with usual care, while reminders alone had small effects. Most studies were before-and-after comparisons. Few studies reported outcomes for people experiencing homelessness or for contacts needing an interpreter, the groups with the lowest completion in most programs. Studies of testing in shelters were small and short, and none followed contacts beyond 90 days."},{"title":"Measuring contact evaluation completion from case management systems: a data quality study","authors":"Brandt-Mensah K, Tanaka-Laurent A","year":2025,"venue":"Public Health Informatics Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared case management system records with paper files for 600 tuberculosis contacts. Evaluation dates were missing for 14 percent of evaluations in the system but present on paper, most often chest radiograph dates entered by hospital staff. Completion estimated from the system alone was 9 percentage points lower than from paper files. A monthly extract with a data dictionary and a missing-date check reduced the gap to 2 points within three months. The check took about two hours of staff time a month."},{"title":"Statistical process control for public health programs with small monthly counts","authors":"Halvorsen-Quist B, Obi-Lindgren C, Reid-Nakashima V","year":2017,"venue":"Improvement Science Methods","doi":"10.5555/ism.2017.0104","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Public health programs often chart outcomes with small monthly subgroups. We show that p-charts with monthly subgroups under 30 give wide, unstable limits, while grouping contacts into cohorts by the month the index case was notified and charting completion at a fixed interval gives stable subgroups of about 100 in a mid-sized program. Run chart rules detected a sustained 12-point improvement within five to six monthly cohorts in simulations. Cohorts must be closed only after the full follow-up interval has passed."}]}
